newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin flies south on second stage of holiday.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin flies south on second stage of holiday.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, jokingly calling himself Boris the First, headed for a holiday resort by Russia's Volga river on Friday after nearly two weeks relaxing near the border with Finland.

The 66-year-old president left northwestern Russia for the Volzhsky Utyos sanatorium once used by Soviet leaders on a lake near Togliatti, 800 km (500 miles) southeast of Moscow. The Kremlin did not say how long he would stay there.

"No Russian leader had come here on holiday since (18th century ruler) Peter I. Now Boris the First has been," Russian television showed Yeltsin telling reporters before flying out of the Karelia region where he had been staying.
Yeltsin's firm grip on power, and his often fatherly manner, have often drawn comparisons with Russia's former tsars.
The president, who had heart surgery last November, looked well and relaxed. "The nature was beautiful, the air was beautiful. I slept wonderfully," said Yeltsin.
Despite being out of Moscow since July 6, Yeltsin has remained the focus of political life, interrupting his routine of fishing, swimming and steam baths to tackle matters of state.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has been running affairs in Moscow in his absence. Visiting Brussels on Friday, Chernomyrdin said Russia hoped to join the European Union soon.
"In the near future, I think that Russia should be in the EU with all the implications and consequences, not all of which will be easy for us," Chernomyrdin told a news conference.
Russian entry to the EU is widely seen as a distant prospect but Chernomyrdin's view reflected the growing confidence of Russia's government as economic reforms start to take effect.

The government, which must repay trillions of roubles (billions of dollars) in unpaid wages to public sector workers such as teachers and doctors, has said it would not have to borrow money to pay the arrears.
"We are sure that the liablities that the government has undertaken will be completely fullfilled," First Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin told a news conference in Moscow.
Yeltsin, anxious to prevent anger swelling over the huge backlog of wages, has also promised to pay off wage arrears to the demoralised armed froces and to start military reforms.
Under decrees which he signed on Wednesday, troop numbers are to be cut by 500,000 to 1.2 million by the end of 1998 and some forces will merge. Critics hit back at his plans on Friday.

Igor Rodionov, sacked by Yeltsin as defence minister in May for failing to start military reforms, said Yeltsin's approach to the reforms "destabilises the situation." Alexander Lebed, fired as Yeltsin's security aide in October, was also sceptical.

"The failure to answer several questions prevents me from feeling optimisitic about the president's latest decree," Lebed said in a written statement casting doubts on funding and the mechanisms for implementing and checking the reforms.
Yeltsin also faces pressure on all sides, including from Pope John Paul II and the U.S. Senate, over a controversial bill restricting religious minorities.

Yeltsin has 14 days to sign or veto the bill "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Association" passed by parliament. The foreign ministry said he would sign it only if legal experts ruled it complied with the constitution and human rights rules.

The Russian Orthodox Church, whose support is a useful part of Yeltsin's armour, supports the bill. But the U.S. Senate has voted to cut off aid if he signs it and the Pope has said the bill threatens the Roman Catholic Church's survival in Russia.
